planting.note: Tuck nursery-propagated crowns into crevices of a well-drained rock garden or scree bed in gritty, lean soil; this circumboreal cliff-dweller resents rich, wet garden soil and needs sharp drainage above all else.

directions: Plant in narrow rock crevices or a scree garden with sharp drainage, mimicking the talus slopes and cliff faces this arctic-alpine species naturally colonizes across Canada, Alaska, and disjunct outposts in New England and the Rockies. The tiny tufted fronds are marcescent, curling inward and persisting through winter as an insulating skirt around the new growth, and release a resinous, apple-like fragrance when crushed, giving the species its common name. Keep it lean and dry between waterings rather than treating it like a typical moisture-loving woodland fern, since excess humidity around the crown promotes rot. Division is slow and best done in spring on well-established clumps.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

common_name: Rocky Mountain Sword Fern (Rock Sword Fern)

planting.note: Set divisions among rock crevices or in gritty, sharply drained soil in a rock garden; this western native tolerates serpentine and other mineral-poor soils that discourage many other ferns.

directions: Grow in rocky, mineral, sharply drained soil in part sun, echoing the serpentine outcrops and open rocky slopes it inhabits from British Columbia and the Klamath ranges east to scattered sites in Idaho and Montana. Compact and narrower-fronded than its larger relative Polystichum munitum, it forms tidy evergreen tufts well suited to a rock garden crevice or dry-stacked wall rather than a shaded, humus-rich fern bed. It is notably tolerant of nutrient-poor, heavy-metal-laden soils that few other ferns can handle, making it a useful choice for lean, gravelly sites. Divide established clumps in spring and expect slow re-establishment.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Wedge divisions into rock crevices or a trough garden with very sharp drainage; this diminutive fern is a specialist of cliff cracks and rock outcrops, not ordinary garden beds.

directions: Best grown in a rock garden crevice, trough, or dry-stacked wall filled with gritty, fast-draining mix, replicating the cliff cracks and serpentine outcrops of the Pacific Northwest and disjunct Rocky Mountain sites where it grows. Named for botanist Arthur Kruckeberg, who studied its unusual tolerance of mineral-poor serpentine substrates, it forms small, stiff, leathery tufts with holly-like pinnae rarely more than a few inches tall. Its extreme miniature scale and preference for near-vertical rock crevices make it a specimen for dedicated rock gardeners rather than a general woodland planting. Handle divisions gently, as the wiry rhizomes establish slowly.

planting.note: Tuck small divisions into limestone or other calcareous rock crevices with excellent drainage; this is the smallest North American Woodsia and needs alkaline, mineral soil rather than typical acidic woodland duff.

directions: Grow in shallow crevices of limestone or other calcareous rock with sharp drainage, matching the arctic and alpine cliff habitat this species occupies from Alaska and arctic Canada south to disjunct calcareous outcrops in the Adirondacks and New England. It is the smallest Woodsia species native to North America, forming delicate deciduous tufts only an inch or two tall that lack the glandular hairs typical of related species, giving smooth fronds. Because it depends on alkaline mineral substrate, avoid amending with acidic organic mulch and instead top-dress with limestone grit. It is best suited to a cold-climate rock garden or crevice trough rather than a conventional fern border.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Transplant rooted stem sections with attached soil and leaf litter into cool, acidic, moist, humus-rich woodland soil in shade; like other clubmosses it depends on native soil fungi and is very slow to establish from division.

directions: Plant rooted sections of the creeping stem into consistently cool, moist, acidic duff beneath conifers or mixed boreal forest, the habitat it favors across Canada, the Great Lakes region, New England, and high-elevation forests further south and west. The stiff, spine-tipped leaves that clothe both the trailing stems and the erect, cone-bearing fertile shoots distinguish it from the softer-leaved Lycopodium clavatum. Because it relies on an intact mycorrhizal partnership in undisturbed forest soil, transplants establish very slowly and often fail if the surrounding leaf litter and fungal community are disturbed too much. It works best as a slow-spreading groundcover in an established shaded woodland garden rather than a bed prepared with typical amended soil.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Transplant rooted sections with intact native soil into lean, acidic, sandy or rocky woodland soil in sun to part shade; it colonizes dry barrens and open pine woods and dislikes rich, wet garden soil.

directions: Establish rooted stem sections in dry, acidic, sandy or rocky soil in an open woodland edge or barren, the sun-exposed habitat where this frosty blue-green clubmoss naturally spreads across eastern Canada and the Appalachians. Its flattened, fan-shaped branches resemble a miniature cedar seedling and give the plant its common name, with slender upright stalks bearing narrow cone-like strobili in late summer. Unlike many clubmosses that prefer deep shade, this species tolerates considerably more sun and drier soil, making it useful for a dry native barrens planting. As with other clubmosses, it depends on soil mycorrhizae and spreads very slowly from transplanted sections.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Tuck small divisions with attached moss and rock grit into a cool, humid, acidic crevice garden in partial sun; this is a high-elevation alpine specialist that rarely survives typical garden conditions.

directions: Plant small tufted divisions among damp, mossy rock in a cool, humid, acidic microclimate that mimics the subalpine and alpine rock outcrops of the White Mountains, Adirondacks, and Gaspe Peninsula where it grows. It forms low, dark green rosette-like tufts closely related to the more widespread Huperzia lucidula but smaller and adapted to colder, more exposed sites. Because it depends on cold temperatures, near-constant humidity, and specific soil fungi found in undisturbed alpine turf, it is exceptionally difficult to establish outside its native elevation and is best treated as a specialist collector's plant for a shaded alpine trough rather than a general garden fern ally. Never collect from wild alpine populations, which are slow-growing and easily damaged.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in fall in lean, moist meadow or open woodland-edge soil in full sun to part shade; like other grapeferns it depends on soil mycorrhizae and is slow and unreliable to establish from division.

directions: Site in open meadows, pastures, or grassy woodland edges with lean, moist soil, the disturbed-to-semi-open habitat this circumboreal species favors across Canada and the northern United States. A single leathery, evergreen, finely divided sterile blade lies close to the ground while a separate upright fertile spike bears clustered, grape-like sporangia, giving the plant both its common name and its distinctive two-part structure. It is one of the more cold-hardy grapeferns and can persist as a green rosette through winter in favorable sites. As with all Botrychium species, it relies on a specific underground mycorrhizal partnership that is extremely difficult to replicate in cultivation, so transplants are slow, often short-lived, and best attempted only with nursery-propagated material rather than wild-collected plants.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
